opening.headline: The reason why the operation service continues to use the previous version even though the model version has been changed is explained by the relationship between the registry, alias, and serving endpoint.
body: The new model has been registered as version 3 and has been verified. However, version 2 is numbered in the service code, so the new version registered is not reflected in operation. Moreover, there are many ways to check which service is running which version. Registering a model and reflecting it in operation are two different things.

In this lesson, we'll first see that the Unity Catalog model registry manages names, versions, and permissions, and that aliases are responsible for deployment status. Next, we compare the fact that the serving endpoint is a different layer from the registry, Snowflake's model registry and container serving in the same framework, and examine the general principles of how new versions are reflected in actual serving and safe promotion strategies such as Canary and Blue-Green. Lastly, we explain the process of changing a service with a hard-coded version number to the alias method.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe relationships between model registries, aliases, and serving endpoints
Version reference method, promotion, and rollback path can be distinguished.
Explain how serving instances reflect new model versions and the differences between canary and blue-green strategies.

screens.title: I changed the version, but the operation uses the previous version.
screens.lead: Select the arrows in the picture one by one to see which version number each service references, and why the new version is not reflected.

visual.alt: Illustration of model versions 1, 2, and 3 in the registry and three services linked directly by version number.

items.prompt: The new model was registered as version 3
items.answer: Registering training results in a registry creates a new model version. Registration means storing model files and metadata, and it has not yet been decided which services will use this version.

items.prompt: The service code is numbered version 2.
items.answer: If a service specifies a model directly as a version number, such as `models:/name/2`, the service will continue to read 2 no matter what new version comes into the registry. Number references are static references unless the service changes.

items.prompt: There are scattered ways to check who is running which version of the service.
items.answer: If your references are scattered across your code, configuration files, and deployment scripts, you won't be able to see the current operating version all at once. When an accident occurs, the response is delayed because we have to first investigate which service is using which version.

items.prompt: Result: Ten promotions and rollbacks need to be fixed.
items.answer: To use a new version, you have to change the code or settings of all callers, and to revert, you have to repeat the same process. This class covers how to reduce this burden with one move.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the structure of the problem, let us recall a similar experience.

screens.title: To recall: what it means to distribute
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: After changing the model version, the operating service continues to use the previous version. Have you ever seen a similar situation?
items.answer: If you have uploaded a new model and the results are the same, and you have been looking for the cause for a while, the service is usually pointing to an older version. You need to get into the habit of checking what the service is reading before checking whether the model has changed.

items.prompt: Was registering a new model and implementing it into operations the same thing?
items.answer: The two are different things. Registration is storage, and reflection is making operational traffic use that version. The device that distinguishes the two is the environment (catalog) and the alias, which indicates the deployment status.

items.prompt: Did you know how to revert to the previous model if something went wrong?
items.answer: If the reversal process is the same size as the promotion process, it will take a lot of time in case of an accident. The best rollback is to revert only one reference to the previous version.

screens.outro: First, let's look at how the registry manages models.

screens.title: Unity Catalog Model Registry
screens.lead: By selecting the number marker in the picture you can see an explanation of what each layer of the model name is responsible for and what it means in the prod catalog.

visual.alt: Unity Catalog model name structure with catalog, schema, model, and version organized into a hierarchical tree.

markers.label: catalog
markers.title: Catalog represents environment and governance
markers.body: Models in Unity Catalog are managed with three level names: Catalog.Schema.ModelName. The fact that it is in the prod catalog only indicates the environment and governance rules and does not mean that it receives operational traffic. Permissions are inherited at the catalog and schema levels, so in prod you can leave only administrators able to delete.

markers.label: schema
markers.title: Schemas tie together teams and project units
markers.body: A schema is an intermediate unit that groups related models. Unity Catalog benefits such as access control, auditing, lineage, and model search across multiple workspaces are centralized on top of this hierarchy.

markers.label: model
markers.title: A registered model is a unit of name and authority.
markers.body: A registered model has a name and is a container for multiple versions. Since it is compatible with the MLflow Python client, you can connect the code you used with the open source MLflow.

markers.label: version
markers.title: When you register learning results, a new version is created.
markers.body: Each time you register a trained model, a new model version is created. A version is an immutable record with a fixed number. The version itself does not say whether it is operational or candidate.

markers.label: alias
markers.title: Deployment status is managed with model alias.
markers.body: Use model aliases to manage deployment status. The key to this screen is that the environment is represented by the catalog and the deployment status is represented by the alias.

screens.outro: Let's take a closer look at the alias responsible for deployment status.

screens.title: alias: named mutable reference
screens.lead: The code below shows the flow of attaching the Champion alias to version 1, moving it to version 2, and then returning it again. Select a range of lines from the description on the right to read what each part means.

data.code:
from mlflow import MlflowClient
import mlflow

client = MlflowClient()
name = "prod.ml_team.iris_model"

#Add Champion alias to version 1
client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "Champion", 1)

#Move the same alias to version 2
client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "Champion", 2)

#Production workloads read models by alias, not by number
uri = "models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model@Champion"
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(uri)

#Rollback: Revert an alias to a previous version.
client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "Champion", 1)

notes.note: Prepare your MLflow client and registered model name. The name has the format Catalog.Schema.Model. If any part of the name is incorrect, the model will not be found.

An alias is a named variable reference that points to a specific version of a registered model. Here, we'll add Champion to the version 1 we're running. The alias is used to indicate deployment status.
If you reassign the same alias to a different version, the object it points to will move. This move is a promotion. The model itself in versions 1 and 2 does not change.

Production workloads read aliases in the form `models:/name@Champion` instead of numbers. When Champion points to a new version, the batch inference workload automatically writes the new version on the next run. You'll need to check separately when servings that are already floating will read the new version.

Reassigning an alias to a previous version is a rollback. This is the quickest route back in the event of an accident since there is no need to change the call destination. This move must be accompanied by permissions and records.

screens.outro: Let's see how the alias moves through the serving layer.

screens.title: Model Serving and Serving Endpoints
screens.lead: Select two floors alternately and compare which objects the same promotion changes on which floor.

visual.alt: A schematic diagram in which the alias of the registry layer and the endpoint of the serving layer are divided into two layers, upper and lower.
labels: Separate operation determines which version to serve

states.label: registry layer
states.body: This layer holds model versions and moves aliases. Moving Champion from version 2 to version 3 involves changing references in the registry, managing names, permissions, and records. This operation alone does not cause already-floating serving endpoints to serve the new version.

states.label: serving floor
states.body: Model Serving deploys your model as a REST API endpoint, allowing you to query it through a single interface. Models learned from Databricks, Foundation Model API, and externally hosted models are managed in the same serving screen, and permissions, usage limits, and quality monitoring by endpoint are centrally handled. It automatically increases and decreases to meet demand, reducing costs. Changing the model version pointed to by an endpoint is a different operation than changing an alias in the registry, and requires a separate deployment workflow to read the alias and update the endpoint. The entity that created the endpoint is recorded as the creator and is used to access Unity Catalog resources.

screens.outro: Let's compare Snowflake to see how the same concept appears on other platforms.

screens.title: Model registry and container serving in Snowflake
screens.lead: Read the table to compare how Databricks and Snowflake provide the same concept under different names.

data.caption: Model management comparison between Databricks and Snowflake
rows: Unity Catalog model from catalog.schema.model name.
It is managed on a schema basis and expressed as Registry, Model, and ModelVersion classes.
The version is indicated by a ModelVersion object.
Permissions inherited from catalogs and schemas
USAGE is used for warehouse inference, READ is used for container inference and metadata viewing.
Create a model service using ModelVersion's create_service and deploy it to Snowpark Container Services.
Automatically scales to meet demand with serverless compute
The service runs in a pre-created compute pool, and ingress must be turned on for external calls.
data.notes: In Snowflake, GPU models are recommended to be scaled by selecting the smallest GPU node that contains the model and increasing the number of instances. Creating a service for a new model can take up to 10 minutes for CPU models, up to 20 minutes for GPU models, or longer if the compute pool is idle or needs to be resized.

screens.outro: Now let's compare how promotion and rollback differ depending on how the version is referenced.

screens.title: Version reference method and promotion/rollback path
screens.lead: Use the slider to change the reference method and operating status to see how the areas that need fixing change when you deploy and revert to a new version.

stops.body: To use a new version, you must change the code or settings of all callers, and rollback requires repeating the same process. If you have 10 call points, you might need 10 changes to upgrade, 10 rollbacks, and a mix of different versions of each service along the way.

Promotion and rollback are completed by leaving the call destination as is and only moving the alias. The caller only knows the alias name, and the registry knows the version number. Because changes happen in one place, records and permissions are in that same place.

Before promotion, it is also possible to send a maintenance call by attaching a candidate alias only to the verification target. If it passes verification, move the operational alias. The process is simple because candidates and operations are treated in the same way.

The older workspace model registry is a separate system called stage transition. Stages were fixed names, one for each version, so different information, such as environment, validation status, and whether it was rolled out, had to be overlaid in one field. So, MLflow suggested discarding the steps and instructed them to divide them into aliases, which can be freely named and have multiple versions per version, and version tags, which record information such as verification status. Separate deployment references into aliases and state records into tags. The Unity Catalog model uses the alias method, so mixing it with the step transition method can cause confusion and must be used separately. Databricks bundle declares these deployment resource settings in YAML and handles them with validate, deploy, and run.

screens.outro: Now let's move on to the case and solve the problem of a service that hardcodes numbers.

screens.title: Principle of serving reflecting new version and safe promotion strategy
screens.lead: Select each tab to see when the serving instance reads the model, how to switch to a new version, and the differences between Canary and Blue-Green.

visual.alt: A side-by-side diagram comparing the canary method, which splits traffic between the old and new version instances, and the blue-green method, which switches traffic to one of the two environments at once.
labels: Compare failure rates, delays with previous versions
Once verification is complete, switch routers and revert if problems occur.

tabs.label: Read at the start of serving
tabs.body: When a serving instance starts, it usually loads the model file into memory or the GPU, and processes subsequent requests with the loaded model. So, even if you move the alias in the registry, the already running instance will not automatically read other files. Moving an alias is a matter of recording in one place the intention of which version you want to serve, but actually loading that version for an instance is a separate operation. There are two ways to reflect. There is a method to switch traffic after launching a new instance with a new version, and a hot reload method in which the same instance reloads the model. Hot reload is only possible when the server supports it, and while reloading, it can nearly double memory or affect request processing, so in large-capacity models, it is simpler to replace it with a new instance.

tabs.label: rolling replacement
tabs.body: Deployment in Kubernetes creates a new ReplicaSet when the pod template changes and gradually replaces old pods with new ones. If the model version is reflected in the pod template as an image tag or environment variable, the version change becomes a rolling update. Old pods are only brought down once the new pod has advertised its ready state, so probe and graceful shutdown settings must be correct for the request to change without failing. The advantage is that it can be changed without additional environments while maintaining almost the capacity, and the limitation is that the old and new versions respond together while the replacement is in progress.

tabs.label: blue-green
tabs.body: Blue-Green is a method of having two operating environments that are as similar to each other as possible. While one side (blue) receives operational traffic, the other side (green) uploads the new version to verify, and when it is deemed stable, switches the router and sends all traffic to green. The previous environment remains intact, so if something goes wrong, the rollback is complete by reverting the router. The advantage is that there is only one version of the response at any one time. The trade-off is the cost of maintaining two environments, which is significant for GPU services.

tabs.label: canary
tabs.body: Canary exposes a new version to only a portion of the total traffic first. The part that has received the change is the canary and the rest is the comparison target (control), and the signal in the canary section is compared with the control to determine whether to proceed. The signals to compare should be things that reveal a real problem and can be attributed to a change, such as a failed request or added delay. In Kubernetes, the document introduces a pattern of setting up a separate Deployment for each release and operating them side by side using labels such as tracks. If it is a model service, indicators of (assumed) response quality can also be included in the comparison. The advantage is that even if a problem occurs, only a small number of users are affected, and the limitation is that the two versions need time to coexist for a while and enough signals to be compared are accumulated.

tabs.label: combined with alias
tabs.body: Registry layer aliases are not separate from the above strategy, but are an input to it. For example, if the candidate alias is read by a canary instance or green environment, and the production alias is read by a blue or existing instance, then moving the production alias after verification is a record of promotion. A rollback consists of two operations: reverting the alias and reverting to the previous version on the serving layer as well. Bundling these two operations into one procedure avoids inconsistencies where the registry uses an old version but the serving uses a new version.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the principle, let us solve the problem of a service that hard-codes numbers using an example.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Problem with services that hard-code version numbers
screens.lead: Ten services have their versions written directly in `models:/name/2`. Select the right arrow to follow the problem as it is revealed one by one.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: All ten services have their version numbers written down directly, such as `models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model/2`. The registry has versions 1, 2, and 3, and operation is based on version 2.

steps.title: Step 1: New versions are not reflected
steps.body: Even if new version 3 passes validation, the service continues to read 2. No matter how many times I raise the model in the registry, nothing happens to the service. Because of this, there is confusion about uploading the model and still getting the results.

steps.title: Step 2: Mix the versions
steps.body: While changing ten places one by one to 3, some end up writing 2 and others write 3. It is not possible to tell at a glance which service is which version, and if the output formats between services are different, problems arise in the subsystem.

steps.title: Step 3: Rollback is the same thing
steps.body: If something goes wrong with the new version and you want to revert, you have to fix the same ten places again. Fixing and deploying code in ten places during an incident is time consuming and prone to mistakes.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Only the alias is known to the caller, and the registry needs to know the version number. If you put the number in the code, promotions, confirmations, and rollbacks all change the code.

screens.outro: Next, I will explain the procedure for changing promotion and rollback using alias.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Changing promotion and rollback by switching alias
screens.lead: This time, we will explain the procedure for changing the same service to alias method. Select the right arrow to follow the order in which the alias labels move.

steps.title: Step 1: Change references to aliases
steps.body: Change the call destination reference to `models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model@Champion` format. You only need to make this change once. Subsequent promotions and rollbacks do not touch the caller's code.

steps.title: Step 2: Promote after verification
steps.body: After registering and verifying the new version 3, move Champion to 3 with `set_registered_model_alias`. This one move will cause all callers reading the alias to point to the new version.

steps.title: Step 3: Roll back when indicators deteriorate
steps.body: If the indicators of the new version become worse, we return Champion to 2. There is no need to change the call destination and the move is done once. Practicing rollbacks will reduce hesitation in the event of an accident.

steps.title: Step 4: Determine when to read
steps.body: Moving an alias does not mean that all servings will change immediately. Batch inference will read the new version on the next run, serving endpoints will only be reflected if the deployment workflow reads the alias to update it, and Snowflake's container service will only be reflected if the service is re-created. Note in the procedure when each serving reads alias changes.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Promotion is a movement of name. All movements must be recorded and authorized. Keep track of who moved your Champion and when, and limit who can move it.

screens.outro: Let me summarize the key points by combining the two cases.

screens.title: Key points: the role of the registry, alias, and serving
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard.

paragraphs: The model registry manages the model's name, version, permissions, and lineage, while the alias handles deployment status, such as which version is running. The environment is represented by a catalog, and the deployment status is represented by an alias.

The serving endpoint is a separate layer that exposes the model as a REST API. Moving an alias in the registry and changing the version served by a serving are different operations, and you need to check when each serving reads the alias. In Snowflake, you create a service from ModelVersion and deploy it to a container compute pool.

The serving instance usually loads the model at startup, so to reflect the new version, you need to replace it with a new instance or use server-supported reloading. The risk of replacement is reduced by dividing the environment into blue and green, or by first exposing to some traffic with canary and comparing signals.
Instead of hardcoding the number, refer to it as an alias, so promotions and rollbacks are in one place. Movements must be subject to authorization and records.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Registering a model and reflecting it in operation are different. Only the alias knows the call destination, and the registry knows the version number.

screens.outro: Lastly, we will review the terminology with cards.

screens.title: Terminology Review Card
screens.lead: The following flashcards capture six key concepts from this lesson. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

cards.back: A repository that manages models with name, version, permissions, and lineage. Unity Catalog uses the three-level names Catalog.Schema.Model, and Snowflake manages them on a schema basis.

A named variable reference that points to a specific version of a registered model. Used to indicate the status of a deployment, and respecifying it to a different version results in a promotion or rollback.

This is the serving layer that deploys models as REST API endpoints to be queried through a single interface. Since it is a separate layer from the registry, there is also a separate operation to change the version pointed to by the serving.
Manage models on a schema-by-schema basis. USAGE permission is used for warehouse inference, and READ permission is used for container inference and metadata viewing.
A call that creates a model service from Snowflake's ModelVersion and deploys it to a compute pool in Snowpark Container Services. Ingress must be turned on to make external calls.

Canary exposes the new version to only a portion of the traffic first and compares the signal with the previous version. Blue-Green creates another environment similar to the operating environment, switches routers after verification, and returns if a problem occurs.

glossary.def: A repository that manages model versions along with their names, permissions, and metadata.
A named variable reference that points to a specific model version. Used to indicate deployment status.
A serving service that deploys and manages models as REST endpoints.
A service that runs container services on top of a compute pool in Snowflake. You can deploy your model service here.
This is a promotion method that exposes the new version to only a portion of the traffic first, compares the signal with the previous version, and then decides whether to expand it.
The method is to create another environment identical to the operating environment and switch routers once the new version is verified. If something goes wrong, we'll revert the router and roll back.

misconceptions.myth: Once you register it in the prod catalog, it has been deployed into production.
misconceptions.fact: The prod catalog only represents the environment and governance rules, not the deployment state. Deployment status is managed with alias.

misconceptions.myth: If you move the alias, all servings change immediately.
misconceptions.fact: In the next run of batch inference, the serving endpoint and container service go through an update process and read the new version. You need to check when each serving reads the alias.

misconceptions.myth: It's clearer and safer if you write the version number down in your code.
misconceptions.fact: If you put the number in, both promotions and rollbacks will be code changes. It is safer if the caller reads the alias and the version number is managed by the registry.

misconceptions.myth: It is simplest and safest to apply the new version all at once.
misconceptions.fact: Applying it all at once ensures that all users are affected if there is a problem. By first exposing only a few with Canary or switching to a verified environment with Blue-Green, risk is reduced and rollbacks are faster.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The registry manages the version, and the alias manages the deployment status.
Serving endpoints and container services are separate layers that expose models.
An alias reference makes promotion and rollback a single move.
Serving usually reads the model at startup, so reflecting a new version requires swapping to a new instance, reducing the risk with Canary or Blue-Green.
